items.title: Focus Question: What happens when a wave reaches the boundary between two media?

answer.html: Part of the wave is reflected back and part is transmitted into the new medium. The frequency stays the same, but the transmitted wave has a different speed and wavelength, and (if it arrives at an angle) a different direction. The incident energy is shared between the reflected and transmitted waves.

items.title: Figure 12 caption: A pulse in a light spring reaches a heavier spring. The incident pulse carries 8.0 J of energy, and the transmitted pulse carries 5.0 J. How much energy does the reflected pulse carry, and how does it compare with the incident pulse?

body.html: Energy is conserved: incident = reflected + transmitted.

answer.html: The reflected pulse carries 3.0 J, less than the incident pulse (about 38% of it), because part of the incident energy went into the transmitted pulse.

items.title: PhysicsLAB: Reflection and Refraction (ripple tank)

question.html: Sample setup: 8.0 Hz straight waves cross from a deep region into a shallow region. The deep region has wavelength 2.4 cm; the shallow region has wavelength 1.5 cm. Find the speeds in each region and describe what you expect for the direction of the waves if they hit the boundary at an angle.

body.html: 𝑓 is set by the source and stays the same. 𝑣= 𝑓𝜆 in each region.

answer.html: 𝑣<sub>deep</sub> = 19 cm/s and 𝑣<sub>shallow</sub> = 12 cm/s. A wave entering the slower shallow region at an angle bends toward the normal, and some of the energy is also reflected, with 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> at a barrier. Your measured values will differ from these sample ones.

check.html: The wave slows in the shallow region and the wavelength shortens by the same factor ( 1.5 / 2.4 = 0.63 and 12 / 19 = 0.63).

items.title: Review the News (Lesson 3)

answer.html: Pick a news story about waves, for example a tsunami warning or a bridge that began swaying. Report the wave type (longitudinal, transverse, or surface), approximate speed or frequency if given, and what happened at boundaries or interference. Then evaluate the source: does it cite measurements, name its sources, and agree with other sources? This is a class task, so write it in your own words.

items.title: Figure 15 caption: Two pulses travel toward each other along a rope: one is 3.0 cm high and upright, the other is 2.0 cm high and inverted. Summarize what the rope looks like when they overlap and after they pass.

body.html: Superposition: displacements add algebraically while the pulses overlap.
At full overlap: +3.0 cm + ( −2.0 cm) = + 1.0 cm.

answer.html: At full overlap the rope has a 1.0 cm upright pulse (partial destructive interference). After passing, each pulse emerges with its original size (3.0 cm up and 2.0 cm down), shape and speed, as if the other were never there.

check.html: Opposite displacements subtract, so the sum is smaller than the bigger pulse.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 3): A standing wave on a guitar string fixed at both ends has 5 antinodes. How many nodes does it have, and what is the displacement at a node?

answer.html: Nodes = antinodes + 1 = 6 nodes (two are the fixed ends). At a node the displacement is always zero.

items.title: Figure 16 caption: A string of length 𝐿= 1.20 m is fixed at both ends. Predict the wavelength of the standing wave at five times the lowest frequency.

body.html: For a string fixed at both ends, 𝑓= 𝑛𝑓<sub>0</sub> goes with 𝜆= 2𝐿/ 𝑛.

answer.html: 𝜆= 0.480 m (that is, 0.4𝐿)

check.html: Five loops of half a wavelength each: 5 ×<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup>

items.title: CCC (Cause and Effect): Describe a ripple-tank procedure to test how the water depth affects the wavelength of waves of a fixed frequency.

answer.html: 1. Set up the ripple tank with a straight-wave generator at a fixed frequency, such as 6.0 Hz. 2. Fill the tank to a depth of 5 mm. Photograph or trace the wavefronts and measure the distance across several wavelengths, then divide to get 𝜆. 3. Repeat for at least five depths (for example 5, 8, 11, 14 and 17 mm), changing only the depth. 4. Compute the speed 𝑣= 𝑓𝜆 for each depth. 5. Graph 𝜆 versus depth. If 𝜆 increases with depth, depth (cause) changes the wave speed and wavelength (effect) while 𝑓 stays fixed.

items.title: Figure 19 caption: Waves of frequency 6.0 Hz travel at 0.18 m/s in shallow water and 0.30 m/s in deeper water. Find the wavelength in each, and say how the wavelength changes as a wave moves from shallow into deep water.

body.html: 𝑓 is the same in both regions, 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓.

answer.html: 𝜆<sub>shallow</sub> = 3.0 cm and 𝜆<sub>deep</sub> = 5.0 cm. Moving into deeper water, the wavelength becomes longer.

check.html: The wavelength grows by the same factor as the speed (0.30 / 0.18 = 1.7).

items.title: 30: A wave on a thin rope travels into a thick rope attached to it. Which characteristics remain unchanged?

answer.html: Only the frequency stays the same. The speed and wavelength change (slower and shorter in the thick rope), the amplitude of the transmitted wave is different from the incident wave (some energy is reflected), and the direction does not change for a rope because it is one-dimensional.

items.title: 31: Sketch two pulses, one 3.0 cm high and the other 4.0 cm high, both on the same side of a rope, that interfere to make a pulse larger than either. How large is the pulse at full overlap?

body.html: Superposition adds displacements: 3.0 cm + 4.0 cm = 7.0 cm.

answer.html: Two upward pulses moving toward each other overlap to make a 7.0 cm pulse at full overlap (constructive interference), then continue unchanged. See the sketch (solid dark curve: the sum; light curves: the individual pulses).

check.html: The sum at overlap is bigger than either pulse alone.

items.title: 32: A water wave moves from deep to shallow water. Under what condition does it enter the shallow region without changing direction?

answer.html: When the wave hits the boundary head-on, meaning the incident ray travels along the normal (𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 0°). The speed and wavelength still change, but the direction does not. If the wave arrives at an angle, it bends (refracts).

items.title: 33: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in a standing wave with 7 nodes (counting both ends). How many antinodes does it have? What fraction of a wavelength is the string's length?

body.html: Nodes = antinodes + 1, and each loop (one antinode between two nodes) is half a wavelength.

answer.html: 6 antinodes, and the string is 3 wavelengths long.

check.html: For 6 loops, 𝜆= 2𝐿/ 6 = 𝐿/ 3, which matches 𝐿= 3𝜆.

items.title: 34 (Critical Thinking): A pulse on a rope is sent toward a point where the rope end is tied to a wall. In another trial, the rope end is tied to a light ring that slides freely on a vertical pole. Which end reflects the pulse inverted, and which reflects it upright? Which situation produces a node at the end?

answer.html: The end tied to the wall cannot move, so it is a node (displacement always zero) and the reflected pulse comes back inverted. The end on the sliding ring moves freely with a large displacement, so it is an antinode and the reflected pulse comes back upright. Only the wall-tied end is a rigid boundary.

check.html: A fixed end forces zero displacement, so the reflected pulse must cancel the incident one at that point, which requires inversion.

items.title: 3D Thinking: Develop and use a model of one wave-power technology (point absorber buoy)

question.html: Choice: Point absorber (floating buoy). Model (what to draw/label): A buoy floating on the surface, connected by a rod or cable to a fixed anchor or heavy plate on the sea floor. As a wave passes, the buoy rises and falls relative to the fixed part. That relative motion drives a hydraulic pump or linear generator. Energy chain: wave energy (kinetic and gravitational PE of the water) → up-and-down motion of the buoy → hydraulic fluid pressure or moving magnets → generator → electrical energy.

answer.html: A labeled sketch showing the buoy, wave direction, anchor, pump or generator, and the energy chain above counts as the model. (An oscillating water column or sea-snake model follows the same pattern: wave motion → relative motion of parts → generator.)

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon and CER: How can a long footbridge that starts swaying when many people walk across it be calmed down?

question.html: Evidence collected in the module: (1) Resonance: forces applied at the natural frequency build large amplitude. (2) A system's natural frequency depends on its properties (for a pendulum, 𝑇= 2𝜋√ℓ/ 𝑔, for a spring, its 𝑘 and 𝑚), so it can be changed. (3) Superposition: motions that are out of phase (opposite displacements) cancel by destructive interference.

body.html: Walkers push at roughly their step frequency. If that matches the bridge's natural frequency, the pushes add in step and the sway grows. A tuned damper moves out of phase with the bridge, so its force opposes the sway (destructive interference), and it absorbs energy. Changing the bridge's stiffness or mass shifts its natural frequency so the pushes no longer match.

answer.html: Installing tuned dampers that oppose the bridge's motion, and adjusting the bridge's natural frequency away from the walking frequency, prevents resonance from building the sway. The evidence supports the original claim. (If your earlier claim differed, revise it using this evidence.)

items.title: STEM Unit Project (Module Wrap-Up): revisit "What's inside the Moon?"

answer.html: Summarize the module evidence for the project: waves change speed (𝑣= 𝑓𝜆 with constant 𝑓) and direction (refraction) and partly reflect at boundaries between materials, and amplitude relates to the wave's energy. Moonquake wave arrival times and the failure of certain wave types to cross a region therefore reveal layer boundaries, including a possible partly molten layer. This is a project task to complete with your class's data.

items.title: Lesson 2: Applying Practices (Wave Characteristics) and Identify Crosscutting Concepts

answer.html: (Applying Practices, online lab, no data provided.) Sample experiment: on a stretched spring toy, measure the wavelength for several frequencies and graph 𝜆 versus 1 / 𝑓; the slope is the speed 𝑣. A sample data point would be 𝑓= 2.5 Hz, 𝜆= 0.80 m, giving 𝑣= 2.0 m/s. Crosscutting-concept table sample: Patterns (regular repeating crests, period and wavelength); Cause and effect (the source's motion sets the wave's frequency); Energy and matter (waves move energy, not matter); Scale (a wave's wavelength can range from nanometers to kilometers).

items.title: Focus Question: What happens when two waves meet?

answer.html: They pass through each other. While they overlap, the displacements add (superposition): constructive interference gives a larger displacement, destructive interference a smaller one. Afterward each wave continues unchanged.

items.title: Figure 12 caption: Compare the energy of the incident wave with that of the reflected wave.

answer.html: The reflected wave carries less energy than the incident wave, because part of the incident energy goes into the transmitted pulse in the second spring. (Incident energy = reflected + transmitted energy.)

items.title: Get It? (node vs. antinode)

answer.html: At a node the medium has zero displacement and does not move at all. At an antinode the medium has the largest displacement.

items.title: Figure 15 caption: Summarize how waves behave during and after superposition.

answer.html: While overlapping, the displacements add algebraically (to larger, smaller, or zero displacement). After the pulses pass, each emerges with its original shape, size, and speed, unaffected by the other.

items.title: Figure 16 caption: Predict the wavelength if the frequency is four times the lowest frequency.

body.html: From the figure, 𝑓= 𝑛𝑓<sub>0</sub> corresponds to 𝜆= 2𝐿/ 𝑛 (see 2𝐿, 𝐿, <sup>2</sup> <sub>3</sub>𝐿).

answer.html: 𝜆=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup>

check.html: Four loops of half a wavelength each: 4 ×<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>𝜆= 2𝐿 with 𝜆= 𝐿/ 2 works out, matching the pattern.

items.title: CCC (Cause and Effect): Procedure for using a ripple tank to test the angle of a barrier versus the angle of the reflected wave

answer.html: 1. Set up the ripple tank with straight waves from the oscillator (constant frequency) and a flat barrier in the water. 2. Place the barrier at a known angle. Draw the normal on paper under the tank. 3. Mark the incident wavefronts and the reflected wavefronts and draw a ray perpendicular to each. Measure 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> and 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub> with a protractor. 4. Repeat for at least five barrier angles (for example 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 75°), changing only the barrier angle. 5. Table or graph 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub> versus 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>. A line of slope 1 supports the cause-and-effect relation 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> (law of reflection).

items.title: Figure 19 caption: How does the wavelength change as the wave travels into shallow water?

answer.html: The wavelength becomes shorter. The frequency stays the same, the speed decreases, and 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓.

items.title: 30: Which characteristics remain unchanged when a wave crosses into a different medium?

answer.html: Only the frequency stays the same. The velocity and wavelength change, the amplitude is reduced (some energy is reflected), and the direction generally changes (unless the wave strikes the boundary head-on).

items.title: 31: Sketch two pulses whose interference gives a pulse bigger than either.

answer.html: Two upward pulses of the same side moving toward each other (for example, 1 cm high each) overlap to make a 2 cm pulse at the moment of full overlap (constructive interference), then continue unchanged. See the sketch (solid dark curve: the sum; light curves: the individual pulses).

check.html: Algebraic sum at overlap is greater than either pulse alone.

items.title: 32: Can 2-D waves cross a boundary without changing direction?

answer.html: Yes. If the wave hits the boundary head-on (rays perpendicular to the boundary, along the normal), the speed and wavelength change but the direction does not. The direction changes only when the wave meets the boundary at an angle.

items.title: 33: Nodes versus antinodes in a standing wave on a string fixed at both ends.

answer.html: There is always one more node than antinodes (nodes = antinodes + 1), since nodes are at both fixed ends and an antinode lies between each pair of nodes. Example: Figure 16 shows 2 nodes and 1 antinode, then 3 and 2, then 4 and 3.

items.title: 34 (Critical Thinking): Covering the right side of the Figure 15 panels at N (left panel) and at A (middle panel).

answer.html: The visible half looks like a pulse reflecting from a boundary at N, which stays at zero displacement, with the reflected pulse inverted. That is exactly the behavior of a rigid wall (fixed end), so yes: the boundary is a rigid wall.

At A (an antinode, maximum displacement) the pulse is reflected upright (not inverted) and the end moves freely with larger displacement. That is a free (non-rigid) end, not a rigid wall, so no, it is not a rigid wall.

check.html: A rigid boundary forces a node and inversion; a free end gives an antinode and no inversion.

items.title: 3D Thinking: Develop and use a model of one wave-power technology

question.html: Choice: Oscillating water column (terminator). Model (what to draw/label): A chamber open to the sea below the waterline with air trapped above, and a turbine in a duct at the top. A rising wave pushes the water column up, forcing air out through the turbine, and the falling water pulls air back in through the same turbine (a turbine that spins the same way both ways), turning a generator. Energy chain: wave energy (kinetic and gravitational PE of water) → motion of the water column (piston) → moving air → turbine's rotation → generator → electrical energy.

answer.html: A labeled sketch/diagram of the chamber, water column, air flow, turbine, and generator with the energy chain above counts as the model. (Point absorber or sea snake models follow the same pattern: wave motion → relative motion of parts → hydraulic pump → generator.)

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon and CER: How can a pendulum save a building from earthquake damage?

question.html: Evidence collected in the module: (1) The period of a pendulum, 𝑇= 2𝜋√ℓ/ 𝑔, can be set by choosing its length, independent of mass. (2) Resonance: forces applied at the natural frequency grow the amplitude. (3) Superposition: waves that are out of phase (opposite displacements) cancel by destructive interference.

body.html: The damper's pendulum is tuned to the building's natural sway period. When the quake drives the building, the heavy bob swings out of phase with the building, so its force opposes the building's motion (destructive interference of the two motions), reducing the amplitude and absorbing the energy.

answer.html: A massive pendulum tuned to the building's natural period moves opposite to the building's sway, subtracting from the vibration amplitude and absorbing its energy, so the building does not build up resonance and is protected from damage. The evidence supports the original claim. (If your earlier claim differed, revise it using this evidence.)

items.title: STEM Unit Project (Module Wrap-Up): revisit "What's inside Earth?"

answer.html: Summarize the module evidence for the project: waves change speed (𝑣= 𝑓𝜆 with constant 𝑓) and direction (refraction), and partially reflect at boundaries between materials, and the amplitude gives the wave's energy. Seismic wave data therefore reveal layer boundaries, which is the unit project's evidence. This is a project task to complete with your class's data.

The weight is "unmarked," so 𝑚 is unknown. Not usable. (A mass on a spring oscillates with the same period on any planet.) Instrument C (pendulum, ℓ= 0.500 m, 47 swings in 1.00 min):

answer.html: Instruments A and C can determine 𝑔; B cannot. Using C, 𝑔≈12.1 N/kg ( 𝑇= 1.28 s). Answer (Evidence and Reasoning): A gives 𝑔= 𝑣<sub>0</sub> / 𝑡<sub>rise</sub> from a known launch speed. C gives 𝑔 from 𝑇= 2𝜋√ℓ/ 𝑔. B depends on the unknown mass, and a spring's period does not depend on 𝑔.
